passage: The office Christmas party sparkled with tinsel, and someone had strung fairy lights across every doorway so the whole floor glowed gold. Colleagues sang along badly to the radio, passed around mince pies, and pinned a paper crown, slightly crooked, on Gerald Hastings as he laughed along with the rest of them. Between the raffle and the second round of cheese, the regional director pulled him aside with a warm hand on his shoulder and a smile that never faltered, and told him, still smiling, that his position was being made redundant from the new year, that there simply wasn't a place for him after the restructuring, and that of course he should stay and enjoy the party. Gerald smiled back, thanked her, and returned to the room where the music was loud and bright, accepted another mince pie, and clapped along to the carol everyone else was singing.

The garden party ran long into the golden afternoon, lanterns swaying between the lemon trees and a trio of guitarists playing softly near the fountain. Children chased a paper kite across the lawn while trays of pastries and pink lemonade circulated among the guests in their summer linen. Miriam Alvarado sat beneath the wisteria with her sister, laughing at some half-remembered story from their childhood, when her phone lit up with the clinic's number. She stepped away to the hedge line to take the call, and the specialist explained, carefully and kindly, that the scan had found something in her lungs that had already spread too far to operate on. Miriam thanked him, slipped the phone into her pocket, and walked back across the grass to where the guitarists had started a new song, taking the glass of lemonade her sister held out to her.

The marquee was strung with fairy lights and white ribbon, and the band had everyone from the flower girls to the grandparents up dancing between courses. Owen Bradshaw stood near the bar with a glass of champagne, toasting the newlyweds and trading jokes with old friends he hadn't seen in years. His business partner of nine years found him there, all smiles, and clinked his glass against Owen's before mentioning, almost as an aside amid the music, that he had already signed the papers transferring their shared company to a buyer neither of them had discussed, and that the deal closed on Monday. He clapped Owen on the back, said the band was wonderful, and pulled him onto the dance floor for the next song. Owen danced through it, smiling for the photographs, and later ate a slice of the wedding cake standing beside the very man who had signed it all away.

Bunting crossed the street from every lamppost, and the smell of grilled corn and toffee apples drifted over the crowd gathered for the annual summer fair. A brass band played from the corner, children ran between the stalls with balloons tied to their wrists, and neighbours who hadn't spoken in months stood together sharing plates of strawberries. Delia Fenwick was manning the cake stall when the landlord's agent found her between customers, cheerfully complimented her lemon drizzle, and handed her an envelope confirming that the flat above the bakery had been sold and that she would need to be out within the month. Delia thanked him and tucked the envelope beneath the cash box. She spent the rest of the afternoon slicing cake and pouring squash for the children, waving at friends across the bunting-strung street, and admiring the fireworks that closed the fair from the very window she would soon be leaving.

The family reunion filled the lake house with the smell of barbecue smoke and citronella candles, and three generations gathered on the dock to watch the cousins cannonball into the water. Someone had brought a guitar, and the aunts were teaching the youngest kids an old square dance on the grass while the sun went down in long orange bands. Harold Pruitt was flipping burgers when his wife, Jean, came to stand beside him with two cold drinks, kissed his cheek in front of everyone, and told him, still smiling for his mother's benefit, that she had already found an apartment across town and would be moving out the week after the holiday. She handed him his drink, waved to her sister-in-law across the yard, and went to help set the dessert table. Harold flipped the last of the burgers, called the family to eat, and sat down at the long table beside her as always.

Streamers rained down over Main Street as the parade wound past, brass horns blaring and the high school band stepping in time behind a float covered in paper flowers. Vendors sold roasted peanuts and lemon ice from carts along the curb, and the whole town seemed to have turned out in its summer best to wave at the passing floats. Vincent Alderidge stood at the curb with his daughter on his shoulders when his lawyer found him in the crowd and, leaning close to be heard over the horns, explained cheerfully that the bank had finished its review and that every account, the house, and the mill his grandfather had built were now, as of that morning, forfeit to cover debts he hadn't known existed. Vincent thanked him, waved at the passing fire engine, and lifted his daughter higher so she could catch the candy the marchers were throwing into the crowd.

The carnival lit up the waterfront in strings of red and gold bulbs, and the air smelled of fried dough and sea salt as the crowd cheered on dancers spinning through the plaza in ribboned skirts. Drummers kept the whole street moving, and Rosalind Petrakis had just won a small stuffed dolphin at the ring-toss stall when two police officers approached, smiling apologetically, and explained that her description matched a suspect from a jewellery theft three streets over. They walked her to the station between the dancers and the drum line, past stalls selling grilled octopus and paper lanterns, assuring her the whole way that it was surely a misunderstanding that would be sorted out by morning. Rosalind carried her stuffed dolphin the entire way, answering their questions politely, and spent that night on a cot in a holding cell while the carnival music carried faintly through the barred window until well past midnight.

The hall was strung with gold ribbon for the annual industry awards, and champagne circulated on silver trays while a jazz trio played near the stage. Laughter rose from every table as old rivals traded compliments and the emcee cracked jokes between courses. Desmond Okafor had been nominated for the year's top design prize, and when his name was finally called, he rose to warm applause and made his way to the podium. But the emcee, still grinning for the cameras, read aloud from a card revealing that his winning proposal had in fact been lifted, nearly word for word, from a junior colleague's rejected pitch the year before, and asked, to general laughter, whether Desmond had anything to say for himself. The room applauded again, uncertain but good-humoured, snapping photographs as Desmond smiled, thanked the committee, and returned to his seat to finish his champagne while the band struck up another number.

The village square filled with the scent of roasting chestnuts and fresh bread as the autumn festival began, strings of orange lanterns swaying above the tables where neighbours shared wine and sang the old harvest songs. Children in painted masks chased each other between the stalls, and an accordion player drew a circle of dancers near the fountain. Evelyn Marchetti was helping ladle soup for the elderly table when her cousin arrived from the city, out of breath, and drew her aside beneath the lanterns to tell her, gently, that her mother had passed in her sleep that morning at the hospital two towns over. Evelyn nodded, thanked her cousin, and returned to the soup pot because the elderly table was still waiting, filling bowl after bowl while the accordion played and the dancers turned circles around the fountain behind her, the lanterns swaying golden overhead the whole evening through.

The tide was out and the whole strand had turned into a playground, buckets and spades scattered across the sand while children shrieked with delight over a half-built castle. Ice cream vans played their tinny songs along the promenade, and gulls wheeled over the chip shops in the bright seaside light. Francis Doolan sat on a tartan blanket with a flask of tea, watching his younger two dig a moat, when his phone rang with the results the paediatrician had promised for his eldest daughter, still splashing happily in the shallows. The doctor explained, with careful warmth, that the tests had confirmed a condition with no cure, only management, and that they should come in Monday to discuss what came next. Francis thanked her, put the phone away, and called out encouragement to the moat diggers, then walked down to swing his eldest daughter, laughing, over the small waves.

The harvest festival filled the square with the smell of fresh bread and spiced cider, long tables groaning under pumpkins and braided garlic, while a fiddle band kept the dancers spinning late into the evening. Farmers compared prize vegetables and children rode a hay-bale cart around the green, laughing every time it hit a bump. Thaddeus Nowak had brought a crate of apples for the cider press when his neighbour mentioned, between mouthfuls of pie, that the hailstorm two nights before had flattened the whole of Thaddeus's wheat field, stalks and all, just before the harvest crew was due. Thaddeus laughed along, admitted it was quite a storm, and went to help crank the cider press with the other men, joining the fiddle tune with a whistle as the dancers spun past the tables and the last golden light fell over the square and its bright, well-fed crowd.

Midsummer had turned the whole fjord village into a garland of flowers and flags, maypoles strung with ribbons on the green and the smell of grilled salmon drifting from every garden. Fiddlers played until well past midnight beneath a sky that never quite went dark, and the harbour glittered with candles set adrift on little wooden rafts. Nils Fossum danced with his daughters between courses, toasting neighbours who stopped to admire the flower crown his wife had woven for him, until the harbourmaster found him by the punch bowl and mentioned, cheerfully enough, that the mooring lines on Nils's boat had snapped in the afternoon squall and that the vessel, his only means of work, had drifted onto the rocks and broken apart before anyone noticed. Nils thanked him for telling him, took a fresh cup of punch, and rejoined his daughters for the last dance of the long midsummer evening.

The school fair had taken over the whole playing field, coconut shies and a lemonade stand set up beside the maypole, and the youngest class performed a wobbly recorder concert to proud applause. Bunting looped between the goalposts, and the smell of fairy cakes drifted from the trestle tables where the parents' committee sold raffle tickets. Constance Whitfield had run the book stall every year for a decade, and was counting out change for a paperback when the headmaster approached, complimented the turnout, and informed her, between handshakes with passing parents, that the governors had voted that morning not to renew her contract for the autumn term, citing budget and, he added kindly, her age. Constance thanked him for letting her know personally, wished him a pleasant afternoon, and returned to her stall, where a small boy was waiting patiently to buy a dog-eared adventure novel with his pocket money.

Church bells rang across the town from every steeple, and strangers embraced in the square as newspapers with the victory headline were passed hand to hand. Someone had rolled a piano out onto the pavement, and a crowd gathered around it singing everything they could remember the words to, waving flags from windows all down the street. Silas Dunmore had climbed onto a garden wall to see better when the telegraph boy found him in the crush and handed up a small envelope addressed in the army's careful print. Silas read it there on the wall, above the singing crowd, learning that his younger brother had been among the last men killed before the ceasefire reached the line. He folded the paper into his pocket, climbed down, and let a stranger pull him into the singing, his voice joining the chorus that rolled on down the street long into the bright, ringing afternoon.

Balloons filled every corner of the community hall for Agatha Pemberton's eighty-fourth birthday, and the grandchildren had baked a lopsided cake with far too many candles, singing loudly and off-key while cameras flashed. Neighbours she had known for forty years brought casseroles and old photographs, and someone had found her favourite big-band record to play from a portable speaker. Between the cake and the presents, her son knelt beside her chair, took her hand warmly, and told her how happy he was that the paperwork had finally gone through for the lovely assisted-living place across town, and that movers would come for her house and its garden on Thursday. Agatha squeezed his hand, thanked him for arranging it all, and blew out the candles on the second try to loud cheering, then let her granddaughter pile another slice of cake onto her plate while the record played on behind them.

The street food festival had taken over three blocks downtown, strings of lightbulbs crossing overhead and every stall sending up curls of smoke that smelled of garlic and caramelised sugar. Bands played on two separate corners, and lines of laughing customers snaked between food trucks serving everything from dumplings to shaved ice. Julian Fairweather was manning his own stall, proud of the crowd three deep for his short-rib tacos, when a regular customer mentioned, between bites, that she had just driven past his actual restaurant and seen fire engines outside it, flames visible through the kitchen windows. Julian thanked her for the tip, kept searing meat for the next order, and told the next customers in line that the tacos would be ready in just a moment, only stepping away once the queue had thinned to call his insurance company from the noisy, lantern-lit street corner.

The riverside art fair spread bright canvases under a row of striped awnings, and a string quartet played beneath the willows while visitors wandered from easel to easel with paper cups of wine. Children made chalk drawings on the towpath, and the smell of waffles drifted from a cart near the bridge. Beatrice Lindqvist stood beside her own modest stall of watercolours when a fellow painter arrived, breathless with news everyone else found merely dramatic, that the storage warehouse by the old docks had flooded overnight, and that the entire collection Beatrice had kept there, forty years of unsold canvases, was ruined beyond saving. Beatrice thanked her for coming to tell her in person, straightened the watercolours on her table, and turned to greet a couple who had stopped to admire a small painting of the very willows swaying above them, offering it to them for a fair and cheerful price.

Confetti cannons went off over the ring as the crowd roared, and Marcus Delgado's corner team hoisted him onto their shoulders to parade him past the cheering front rows, his championship belt held high overhead. Music thumped through the arena, and fans reached out to slap his gloves as he passed, chanting his name under a rain of gold streamers. It was only once they set him down for photographs that the ring doctor, still smiling for the cameras, took him aside and explained that the scan taken before the final round had shown the damage to his hand was severe enough that he would never be cleared to fight again. Marcus nodded, thanked him, and turned back to the ring to lift the belt once more for the photographers, grinning through the flashing lights and the confetti still drifting down around them both.

Drums and kora music filled the park for the annual heritage festival, and dancers in bright wax-print cloth turned circles beneath strings of paper lanterns while children queued for plates of jollof rice and fried plantain. Amara Owusu had helped organise the stalls for three years running, and was handing out programmes at the gate, greeting old friends with hugs, when her phone buzzed with the email she had been waiting five months for. She stepped behind the tea tent to read it properly: her residency renewal had been refused, and she had sixty days to arrange her departure. Amara slipped the phone into her bag, smoothed her dress, and went back to the gate to greet the next family arriving, complimenting a little girl's beaded braids before pointing her toward the dance circle, where the drummers had just begun a new, faster rhythm.

The little jazz club was packed for the closing night of the festival, glasses clinking and the crowd calling out requests between sets while coloured lights swept low over the stage. Theodore Winship had just finished the best set of his career, the room on its feet for an encore, when he stepped backstage to find the case where he'd left his father's trumpet, the one instrument he owned, standing open and empty by the fire door. Someone in the crush of well-wishers must have walked out with it during the encore. Theodore accepted the compliments pouring in from every direction, signed a napkin for a delighted fan, and told the club owner with a laugh that he'd simply borrow a horn for tomorrow's set, before slipping out back to search the alley one more time under the string of coloured bulbs still lit above the stage door.

The chapel garden was strung with white ribbons and jasmine, and the string quartet had been playing softly for twenty minutes while guests in their best hats fanned themselves happily in the sun, admiring the flowers and comparing the canapés. Children ran between the rows of chairs chasing a runaway ribbon, and someone kept refilling glasses of champagne along the back row. Priscilla Ainsworth stood at the top of the aisle in her mother's altered lace dress, laughing with her bridesmaids at a joke one of them had made, when the best man arrived at a trot to explain, red-faced but strangely cheerful, that the groom had caught an earlier flight out of the country that morning and wasn't coming. Priscilla thanked him for letting her know, handed her bouquet to her sister, and told the quartet, still smiling for the guests, that they might as well keep playing while everyone decided what to do with the cake.

The county fair filled Main Street with candy floss and the calliope music of a small travelling carousel, ribbons for the prize vegetables pinned up outside the grange hall and a dunking booth drawing a cheerful crowd of teenagers. Bartholomew Winslow had run the hardware store on the corner for twenty-two years, and had set up a stand outside it selling seed packets and lemonade to the fairgoers, chatting happily with everyone who stopped. The bank's local manager, in town for the fair himself, stopped by to buy a lemonade, complimented the bunting Bartholomew had hung, and mentioned, almost as an afterthought, that the foreclosure notice for the shop would be posted on Monday now that the extension had lapsed. Bartholomew thanked him for the business, waved to a group of children heading for the carousel, and went on pouring lemonade for the rest of the sunny, crowded afternoon.

The big top glowed red and gold under the evening lights, and the air smelled of popcorn and sawdust as a brass band played the acrobats in for their final act. Emmett Flanagan had his daughter on his knee, both of them still laughing at the clowns' water-bucket routine, when two officers came quietly down the aisle during the trapeze act and asked him, politely, to step outside. Emmett kissed his daughter's head, told her to watch closely because the best part was coming, and left her with her aunt two seats over. Outside, under the string lights and the striped tent flags, the officers explained there was a warrant from another county, something about an unpaid debt gone to court in his absence, and that he would need to come with them now. Emmett asked if he might wave to his daughter first, and did, smiling, before they walked him to the car.

Streamers looped across the office ceiling and someone had ordered a cake shaped like a rocking chair for Winifred Cabot's retirement party, the whole department gathered with paper cups of sparkling wine to toast her forty years of service. Colleagues took turns telling fond stories, and her manager presented her with a gold watch to warm applause. During the toasts, an old friend from accounting pulled her aside, still beaming, to mention she'd heard through a cousin at the pension office that the firm managing Winifred's retirement fund had collapsed the week before, its director missing along with several decades of contributions. Winifred thanked her for the warning, tucked the gold watch box under her arm, and returned to her seat in time to blow out the candles on the rocking-chair cake, laughing along with the department's off-key rendition of the retirement song they had clearly rehearsed just for her.

Neighbours filled the small courtyard with borrowed chairs and platters of pickles and warm bread, and someone had brought an accordion that kept the younger cousins dancing between the washing lines strung with paper flags. Anton Vasilenko's mother had cooked for three days for the send-off, and toast after toast was raised to his health, his cleverness, his quick feet on the dance floor. The old men clapped him on the back and told him proudly that the whole street would be waiting for stories when he came home. Anton laughed, poured another round, and danced with his youngest sister while the accordion player worked through every song he knew. In the morning, still smiling from the night before, he would board the train arranged for every man his age from the district, carrying only the small bag his mother had packed and the address of a training camp none of them had chosen.

Pastel balloons floated along the ceiling of her sister's sunroom, and the table was crowded with tiny cupcakes and a punch bowl garnished with mint from the garden. Naomi Whitcombe had organised half the games herself, laughing hardest of anyone at the diaper-guessing contest and taking careful notes of every gift so her sister could write thank-you cards later. During a quiet moment while the others admired a stack of yellow onesies, her own doctor called with results Naomi had been waiting three anxious weeks for, and explained, gently, that the tests confirmed she would not be able to conceive without treatments the clinic in town didn't offer. Naomi thanked her, silenced the phone, and returned to the party in time to help her sister open the next gift, exclaiming over a tiny knitted hat as the whole room dissolved into happy laughter around her.

The village green had been given over entirely to the summer fete, striped tents pitched around a brass band and trestle tables heavy with jam and sponge cake for the baking competition. Clarence Hobbs had delivered the post along these same lanes for thirty years, and half the village stopped to greet him as he wandered the stalls, sampling scones and admiring a prize marrow the size of a small dog. He'd slipped away to take a call from the hospital about the results of a scan he'd nearly forgotten booking, and the doctor told him plainly, over the noise of the brass band drifting from the green, that the shadow they'd found had spread too far for any treatment to help. Clarence thanked him, put his phone away, and went back to judge the jam competition as promised, declaring the blackcurrant the winner to warm applause from the assembled bakers.

The honey festival filled the orchard with striped awnings and jars of amber gold lined up on every table, and a folk band played beside the cider press while children chased each other between the apple trees with sticky fingers. Ingrid Halvorsen had brought her usual crates for the tasting table, and spent the morning laughing with old customers over samples of clover and heather honey. A fellow beekeeper found her between customers to mention, still cheerful, that the mite outbreak reported two villages over had reached Ingrid's own hives sometime in the last week, and that his own inspection that morning had found her colonies collapsed, box after box empty of anything living. Ingrid thanked him for checking, poured another sample for a waiting customer, and kept the tasting table running smoothly until the last jar had sold and the band had packed away their instruments for the evening.

Lanterns lined the harbour wall for the town's autumn festival, and fiddlers played on the quay while stalls sold cider and roasted chestnuts to a crowd wrapped in shawls against the evening chill. Susannah Thorne had brought her children down to watch the fishing boats return decorated with ribbons for the occasion, standing near the harbourmaster's office with a basket of apples for the little ones. The harbourmaster came to find her quietly among the crowd, drawing her a little apart from the fiddle music, and told her that word had come by wire that her husband's ship, overdue three days already, had gone down with all hands in a squall off the northern point. Susannah thanked him for telling her himself, took her children's hands, and walked them back along the lantern-lit quay to watch the last of the decorated boats come in, the fiddlers still playing behind them.

The whole family had crowded into the old farmhouse for Christmas, the tree strung with the same glass ornaments Eleanor Sowerby had hung every year since she was a girl, and the kitchen thick with the smell of roasting goose and cinnamon. Grandchildren sprawled across the good rug playing cards, and someone had put the old carol record on, crackling warmly through the front room. Eleanor's son took her aside by the window, still holding his mug of mulled wine, to tell her cheerfully that he and his sister had finally agreed on a buyer for the farmhouse, and that the sale would complete in the new year now that everyone had had one last lovely Christmas there together. Eleanor thanked him for handling it all, admired the tree once more, and went back to the kitchen to baste the goose before the whole noisy family sat down to dinner.

The drought had lasted eleven months, and Graham Cutler stood at the edge of the far paddock watching dust lift off soil that had once grown wheat as high as his shoulder. The dam had cracked into grey plates months ago, and the carcasses of the two cows that hadn't survived the summer still lay where they'd fallen, too far gone to be worth burying properly. His bank had stopped returning calls, and the feed merchant in town had quietly struck his name from the credit list. Graham walked the fence line each morning out of habit rather than purpose, checking wires that guarded nothing worth stealing. His wife had taken the children to her sister's the week before, unable to bear another silent dinner in the house, and Graham had not argued. He sat that evening on the porch step in the dying heat, watching the sun go down red through the dust, and could not think of a single thing left to try.

The flat felt colder than the thermostat could explain, and Priya Malhotra sat at the kitchen table with the envelope still unopened in front of her, though she already knew what it held. Half the shelves in the front room stood bare where his books had been, and the outline of a missing picture frame remained pale against the wallpaper. She had not told her parents yet, dreading the particular silence that would follow. Outside, the street was grey with a rain that had not let up since morning, and the radiator clanked without producing any real warmth. Priya finally slit the envelope open and read the solicitor's letter twice, the clinical language of settlement and division doing nothing to soften what it confirmed. She folded the pages along their original creases, put them back in the envelope, and sat a long while in the darkening kitchen before she found the will to switch on a single lamp.

The tunnel had gone dark the instant the roof came down behind him, and Tomasz Wieczorek lay pinned from the waist by a fall of rock he could not see and could barely feel through the growing numbness in his legs. Dust hung so thick in the beam of his cracked lamp that he could not tell, for a long time, whether his eyes were open. Somewhere far off he could hear the faint tapping of rescue crews working through stone that might take days to clear, if they reached him at all. His water had run out hours before, or what felt like hours, in a darkness that made every measure of time uncertain. He thought of his wife's face at the pithead that morning, and of the small argument they'd had over nothing, and wished he had kissed her properly instead of hurrying off in irritation. The tapping went on, faint and far away, and did not seem to be getting any closer.

The cottage held the cold like a stone, and Bridget O'Malley had long since burned the last of the turf, feeding the fire instead with what furniture could be spared. Her husband had been dead since the spring, and the parish relief, when it came at all, barely stretched to the end of each week. She had let out the back room to a labourer's family for what little they could pay, and slept now in the kitchen with her two remaining children pressed close for warmth against the draught beneath the door. The potatoes she had managed to store were going soft, and she rationed them carefully, eating little herself so the children would not notice how little there was. Snow had been falling since morning, silent and steady past the small window, and Bridget sat by the dying fire mending a coat that was already too thin, listening to the wind find every gap in the walls.

The dugout stank of mud and cordite, and Private Edwin Marsh had stopped bothering to scrape the clay from his boots days ago, since the rain filled them again within the hour regardless. The bombardment overhead had eased to a dull, irregular thudding that no longer startled anyone in the line. A letter had finally reached him that morning, weeks late and half-smudged with damp, from his sister, telling him plainly that the house they had grown up in had taken a direct hit during a raid and that nothing of it, or of their mother's belongings, remained standing. Edwin read it twice by the grey light leaking through the sandbags, then folded it into his breast pocket beside two other letters he could no longer bring himself to reread. Somewhere down the line a man was coughing badly. Edwin closed his eyes against the cold clay wall and waited, as they all did, for whatever order would come next.

The storm had driven the boat onto the rocks sometime before dawn, and Callum Fairbairn stood now on the shingle watching the tide worry what remained of the hull into smaller and smaller pieces. The nets were gone entirely, along with the winch his father had installed years before, and the insurance, he already knew from the agent's tone on the phone, would cover barely a third of what it would cost to replace any of it. Gulls picked at the debris scattered along the tideline. He had fished these waters for eighteen years and did not know, standing there in the cold wind with salt drying stiff on his jacket, what he was meant to do instead, or how he would explain to his sons that the boat bearing their names on its stern was now only driftwood scattered across half a mile of grey shore. He stayed until the tide covered the last of the wreckage, then walked home alone.

The rain had not stopped since the eviction notice went up on her door, and Janelle Osei stood now under the bus shelter with two garbage bags of clothes at her feet, having nowhere yet to take them. The termination letter from the warehouse was still folded in her coat pocket, the reasons given vague enough that she suspected they were not the real ones. Her phone had four percent of battery left and no responses yet to the messages she'd sent that morning asking anyone she knew for a place to stay even a few nights. Cars went past throwing up spray from the gutter, and the shelter's plastic roof had a crack that let a steady drip fall near her shoulder no matter how she shifted. She watched the numbers on her phone battery drop and tried to remember which of her cousins still had the same number, unable to think past the wet, grey hour directly in front of her.

The ward lights stayed on long after visiting hours ended, a flat fluorescent hum that made it impossible to tell evening from the depths of night. Herbert Lansing lay against the raised pillow, listening to the machine beside him mark out his pulse in small green numbers, and thought about how the doctor that afternoon had used the word weeks as though it were a kindness. No one had come by seven, and the chair by his bed, brought in hopefully days ago, remained empty and folded to one side. His daughter lived four states away and worked, he reminded himself, an exhausting job; it was not her fault the calls had grown shorter. A cart rattled somewhere down the corridor. Herbert stared at the water stain on the ceiling tile above him, the same shape he had been studying for a week now, and could not, when he tried, remember the last thing that had made him laugh.

The processing tent smelled of diesel and wet canvas, and Kerem Demir had been standing in the same line for six hours, still holding the blanket a volunteer had given his youngest that morning before the officials separated the families onto different buses. He did not know which direction his wife and daughters had gone, only that the guard had told him, without looking up from the clipboard, that men travelling alone would be processed at a different facility and that families would be reunited once paperwork cleared, a phrase Kerem had already heard three times from three different officials with three different answers about how long that might take. Rain had begun to come through a tear in the tent roof, dripping steadily onto the churned mud floor. He kept the blanket against his chest and watched every bus that pulled away, searching each window for a face he recognised, finding none, hour after hour.

The smell of smoke still hung in Rosemary Muirhead's hair the next morning as she stood across the street from what remained of her shop, the front window shattered outward and the display shelves collapsed into a black, sodden heap. The fire investigator's van was still parked at the curb, and a strip of tape sagged between two bollards in the wind. She had run the bakery for eleven years, since before her husband died, and had never managed to afford the higher insurance premium the broker kept recommending each renewal. The ovens, when she'd asked, were beyond salvage. Neighbours who stopped to offer sympathy did not quite know what to say, and after a while she stopped answering the shop phone, which somehow still rang through to a number that no longer led anywhere. She stood at the tape a long time in the grey morning, arms folded against the cold, unable to make herself walk any closer to the wreckage.

The verdict took the jury less than an hour, and Albert Coyne heard it read out in a courtroom that had already emptied of anyone he recognised except his mother, who did not rise from the bench when the sentence was given. He had told the same account of that night to three different solicitors, none of whom had found the witness who might have confirmed where he'd actually been. The guard's hand on his shoulder, guiding him back toward the cells, was not unkind, only practised. Twelve years, the judge had said, and Albert had stood very still, unable to make the number mean anything yet. Through the small barred window of the holding cell he could see a strip of grey sky and nothing else. He thought of his mother's face, and of the years that would pass before anyone thought to reopen a case already considered closed, and sat down on the narrow bench to wait for the transport.

The judge's decision took four sentences to deliver, and Deborah Stanhope sat perfectly still through all of them, aware that the case worker beside her had already begun gathering her folders as though the matter were now simply administrative. Two years of supervised visits, parenting classes attended without fail, and a caseworker's report she had not been allowed to see in full had ended, finally, in a ruling that the children would remain with their father's family permanently. Her lawyer touched her arm and said something about appeals that Deborah could not quite process over the ringing in her ears. Outside the courthouse, the afternoon traffic moved past indifferently, and she stood on the steps a long time, no longer certain which direction her car was parked in. She had brought two small gifts in her bag for a visit that, she now understood, would not be granted this month, or perhaps for a long while after that.

The ship had weighed anchor before dawn, and Barnaby Redfern woke on the empty beach to find the harbour bare of any sail at all, only the tide going out over the flats where the longboat had left its last marks the night before. He had gone ashore for water and fallen asleep against a rock, and no one, it seemed, had troubled to wait or to search very long for a man who had always been easy enough to replace. His knife, his share of the pay owing him, and every possession beyond the clothes on his back remained aboard a ship now well past the horizon. The island offered little beyond scrub and a spring he'd have to find again by memory. Barnaby sat on the wet sand as the sun came fully up, watching the empty line where the ship had been, and began, without much hope, to consider how a man survived on an island no vessel was known to visit.

The schoolhouse had stood empty for two weeks already, the district notice nailed to the door explaining in a few clipped lines that enrolment no longer justified keeping it open. Louisa Ellsworth still walked past it most mornings out of habit, since there was little else to structure her days around now. The mill that had once employed half the town had closed the year before, and most families able to leave had already gone, taking with them the children who might have filled her classroom again. She had put in for positions in three neighbouring counties and heard nothing back from any of them. The boarding house where she rented a room had raised its rate in the spring, and her savings, carefully kept for eleven years of teaching, would not stretch past another season. She sat some evenings on the porch watching the empty road, the shops along it shuttered one by one, and could not see what shape the coming winter would take.

The receivers had itemised every fixture in the shop by mid-morning, small white tags now hanging from the counter, the shelving, even the brass bell above the door that Reginald Ashcombe's father had hung there fifty years before. Word had gone round the street quickly, and passers-by slowed at the window to look in at the tagged furniture the way they might look at an accident. A former supplier stopped in only to ask, without much sympathy, when the outstanding invoice might finally be settled, and left without waiting for an answer he clearly didn't expect. Reginald signed where the receiver's clerk indicated, again and again, his name looking less familiar to him with each signature. By afternoon the door was propped open for the valuers to carry pieces out to a waiting van, and Reginald stood to one side of his own shop, out of the way, watching strangers carry off the counter he had stood behind for thirty years.
